The segments in @sec-cluster were built from purchase behaviour only. Demographics were deliberately left out of the clustering, so that the groups describe *how* households buy rather than *who* they are. This section brings the demographics back in to answer the client's next question: who are the households in each segment, and how can they be reached?

## Which three demographics, and why

Each variable was chosen because a difference between segments on it leads to a different business action.

```{r}
#| label: profile-var-choice

# The three demographics used to profile the segments
profile_vars <- c("SEC", "HS", "AGE")

# Missing values per profile variable (zeros were turned into NA in section 07)
profile_missing <- soap_clean |>
  summarise(across(all_of(profile_vars), \(x) sum(is.na(x)))) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable", values_to = "n_missing")

tibble(
  variable = profile_vars,
  type     = c("Ordinal, 1 high to 4 low", "Numeric, number of members", "Ordinal, 1 young to 4 old"),
  action   = c("Price point and premium or economy range",
               "Pack size and multi-packs",
               "Media channel and message")
) |>
  left_join(profile_missing, by = "variable") |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(variable = "Variable", type = "Type", action = "Business lever it informs",
             n_missing = "Missing households") |>
  tab_header(title = "The three profiling demographics")
```

- **SEC (socioeconomic class)** tells a manufacturer what price a segment can bear. If the loyal, heavy buyers are mostly high SEC, a premium range and loyalty rewards suit them; if the promotion-led buyers are mostly low SEC, price discounts are the right tool. SEC is also one of the strata the panel was sampled on, so all `r nrow(soap_clean) - profile_missing$n_missing[profile_missing$variable == "SEC"]` households have a value.
- **HS (household size)** is the demographic most directly tied to how much soap a household uses. It tells the client which segments should be offered larger packs or multi-packs. `r profile_missing$n_missing[profile_missing$variable == "HS"]` households have no size recorded and are left out of the HS summaries only.
- **AGE (age of the homemaker)** tells an advertising agency where and how to speak to each segment, for example television versus newer channels, and what message will land. Every household has a value.

The three variables point to three *different* levers (price, pack, media), so together they give a client a fuller plan than three variables that all say the same thing.

```{r}
#| label: other-demographics

# Facts used to explain why the other demographics were not chosen
other_missing <- soap_clean |>
  summarise(across(c(FEH, MT, SEX, EDU, CHILD, CS, Affluence), \(x) sum(is.na(x))))
share_female  <- mean(soap_clean$SEX == 2, na.rm = TRUE)
share_tv      <- mean(soap_clean$CS == 1, na.rm = TRUE)   # used later for the media advice
# Spearman correlation, because SEC is ordinal
sec_aff_cor   <- cor(soap_clean$SEC, soap_clean$Affluence, method = "spearman", use = "complete.obs")
```

**Why not the others.** `Affluence` is a strong candidate, but it overlaps with SEC (Spearman correlation `r round(sec_aff_cor, 2)`; SEC runs from 1 high to 4 low, so a negative value means wealthier households sit in the higher classes) and has `r other_missing$Affluence` missing households, so it would repeat SEC's message with less data. `MT` (native language) and `CHILD` are codes with no labels in the data guide, so a difference could not be turned into an action. `SEX` barely varies: `r percent(share_female, accuracy = 1)` of homemakers with a recorded value are female. `EDU`, `FEH` and `CS` are missing for `r other_missing$EDU`, `r other_missing$FEH` and `r other_missing$CS` households respectively and are less directly linked to a bath soap decision than the three chosen. @sec-profile-check tests this choice against the data.

**Missing values.** No household is dropped from the segmentation. For HS, each summary and test uses the households that have a value, and the number used is shown.

## Profile by group

```{r}
#| label: profile-data
#| eval: true

# Attach the three demographics (and TotalVol, to link size to volume) to each household's segment
profile_df <- soap_clusters |>
  select(MemberID, cluster) |>
  left_join(soap_clean |> select(MemberID, all_of(profile_vars), TotalVol), by = "MemberID") |>
  mutate(
    # Give the ordinal codes readable labels for the charts
    SEC = factor(SEC, levels = 1:4, labels = c("1 High", "2", "3", "4 Low")),
    AGE = factor(AGE, levels = 1:4, labels = c("1 Young", "2", "3", "4 Old"))
  )

# One chart function for both categorical variables, so they look the same
plot_props <- function(data, var, title) {
  data |>
    filter(!is.na({{ var }})) |>
    count(cluster, {{ var }}) |>
    group_by(cluster) |>
    mutate(prop = n / sum(n)) |>                 # share within each segment
    ungroup() |>
    ggplot(aes(cluster, prop, fill = {{ var }})) +
    geom_col(colour = "white") +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = percent) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = pal) +
    labs(title = title, x = "Segment", y = "Share of households in the segment", fill = NULL)
}

# Small helpers that let R write the interpretation, so no number is typed by hand
seg_label <- function(k) {
  # Use Shrrii's segment name if section 08 provides one
  if ("segment" %in% names(soap_clusters)) {
    nm <- soap_clusters |> filter(cluster == k) |> pull(segment) |> first()
    as.character(str_glue("Segment {k} ({nm})"))
  } else {
    as.character(str_glue("Segment {k}"))
  }
}
pct   <- \(x) percent(x, accuracy = 1)
fmt_p <- \(p) if_else(p < 0.001, "p < 0.001", paste("p =", sprintf("%.3f", p)))
```

```{r}
#| label: profile-tests-compute
#| eval: true

# Cramer's V: chi-squared rescaled to run from 0 (no association) to 1
cramers_v <- function(tab, stat) sqrt(stat / (sum(tab) * (min(dim(tab)) - 1)))

# Chi-squared test plus Cramer's V for one categorical variable
chisq_row <- function(data, var) {
  d   <- data |> filter(!is.na(.data[[var]]))
  tab <- table(d$cluster, d[[var]])
  res <- chisq.test(tab, simulate.p.value = TRUE, B = 5000)   # simulated p-value, see below
  tibble(variable = var, test = "Chi-squared", n = sum(tab), p_value = res$p.value,
         effect = cramers_v(tab, unname(res$statistic)), effect_measure = "Cramér's V")
}

# Label an effect size in words. The usual cut-offs differ by measure:
# Cramer's V 0.1 / 0.3 / 0.5, epsilon squared 0.01 / 0.08 / 0.26.
effect_word <- function(effect, measure) {
  cuts <- if (measure == "Cramér's V") c(0.1, 0.3, 0.5) else c(0.01, 0.08, 0.26)
  case_when(effect < cuts[1] ~ "negligible", effect < cuts[2] ~ "small",
            effect < cuts[3] ~ "moderate", TRUE ~ "large")
}

hs_df <- profile_df |> filter(!is.na(HS))       # only households with a recorded size

set.seed(55789)   # the simulated p-values are random, so fix them
kw_hs <- kruskal.test(HS ~ cluster, data = hs_df)

profile_tests <- bind_rows(
  chisq_row(profile_df, "SEC"),
  tibble(variable = "HS", test = "Kruskal-Wallis", n = nrow(hs_df),
         p_value = kw_hs$p.value,
         effect = unname(kw_hs$statistic) / (nrow(hs_df) - 1),    # epsilon squared
         effect_measure = "Epsilon squared"),
  chisq_row(profile_df, "AGE")
) |>
  mutate(size       = map2_chr(effect, effect_measure, effect_word),
         actionable = p_value < 0.05 & size != "negligible",
         verdict    = case_when(
           actionable      ~ str_glue("statistically significant and {size} in size, so it is a usable guide for targeting"),
           p_value < 0.05  ~ "statistically significant but negligible in size, so it should not drive decisions on its own",
           TRUE            ~ "not statistically significant, so the pattern in the chart may be chance and should not be used for targeting"
         ))

# One sentence on the test result, reused under each chart
test_sentence <- function(var) {
  r <- profile_tests |> filter(variable == var)
  test_name <- if_else(r$test == "Chi-squared", "chi-squared", r$test)   # lower case mid-sentence
  str_glue("The {test_name} test ({fmt_p(r$p_value)}, {r$effect_measure} = {round(r$effect, 3)}) shows this difference is {r$verdict}.")
}
```

## Are the differences real?

A chart can show a difference that is only noise. Each variable is therefore tested. SEC and AGE are categorical, so a chi-squared test of independence checks whether the mix of classes differs between segments. Some AGE cells are small (few households have the youngest code), so the p-value is simulated rather than taken from the chi-squared table, which stays valid when expected counts are below 5. HS is a count with a long right tail, so the Kruskal-Wallis test, which compares the segments on ranks rather than means, is used instead of ANOVA.

A small p-value only says a difference exists. With 600 households even a tiny difference can be "significant", so an effect size is also reported: Cramér's V for the categorical variables and epsilon squared for HS. Both run from 0 (no association) to 1. The usual guide is that Cramér's V below 0.1 is negligible, from 0.1 small, from 0.3 moderate and from 0.5 large; for epsilon squared the same steps are 0.01, 0.08 and 0.26.

```{r}
#| label: profile-tests
#| eval: true

profile_tests |>
  select(variable, test, n, p_value, effect, effect_measure, size) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(effect, decimals = 3) |>
  fmt_number(p_value, decimals = 4) |>
  cols_label(variable = "Variable", test = "Test", n = "Households used",
             p_value = "p-value", effect = "Effect size", effect_measure = "Measure",
             size = "Size") |>
  tab_header(title = "Do the segments differ on each demographic?")
```

## Where do the differences come from?

A significant test says the segments differ *somewhere*, not where. Two follow-up checks locate the difference.

For SEC and AGE, the **standardised residual** of each cell compares the number of households in that segment and class with the number expected if the segments had the same mix. A value beyond ±2 marks a cell with clearly more (positive) or fewer (negative) households than expected.

```{r}
#| label: profile-residuals
#| eval: true
#| fig-width: 10

# Standardised residuals of the segment by class table, in long form for plotting
resid_df <- function(data, var) {
  d   <- data |> filter(!is.na(.data[[var]]))
  tab <- table(cluster = d$cluster, level = d[[var]])
  # only the residuals are used here, so the small-count warning about the p-value does not apply
  res <- suppressWarnings(chisq.test(tab))
  as.data.frame.table(res$stdres, responseName = "resid") |> mutate(variable = var)
}

plot_resid <- function(rd, title) {
  ggplot(rd, aes(level, cluster, fill = resid)) +
    geom_tile(colour = "white") +
    geom_text(aes(label = round(resid, 1), colour = abs(resid) > 2), show.legend = FALSE) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "white", `FALSE` = "black")) +   # readable on dark tiles
    scale_fill_gradient2(low = pal[4], mid = "white", high = pal[1], midpoint = 0) +
    labs(title = title, x = NULL, y = "Segment", fill = "Residual")
}

sec_resid <- resid_df(profile_df, "SEC")
age_resid <- resid_df(profile_df, "AGE")

plot_resid(sec_resid, "Socioeconomic class") +
  plot_resid(age_resid, "Age of the homemaker") +
  plot_annotation(caption = "Purple: more households than expected. Green: fewer. Beyond ±2 is a clear difference.")
```

For HS, **pairwise Wilcoxon tests** compare every pair of segments. The Holm adjustment corrects the p-values for making several comparisons at once, so the chance of a false "difference" stays at 5% overall.

```{r}
#| label: profile-hs-pairs
#| eval: true

hs_pairs <- pairwise.wilcox.test(hs_df$HS, hs_df$cluster,
                                 p.adjust.method = "holm", exact = FALSE) |>
  tidy()

hs_pairs |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(p.value, decimals = 4) |>
  cols_label(group1 = "Segment", group2 = "Compared with", p.value = "Holm adjusted p-value") |>
  tab_header(title = "Household size: which pairs of segments differ?")
```

```{r}
strong_cells <- bind_rows(sec_resid, age_resid) |>
  filter(abs(resid) > 2) |>
  arrange(desc(abs(resid)))
sig_pairs <- hs_pairs |> filter(p.value < 0.05)

cells_text <- if (nrow(strong_cells) == 0) {
  "No cell in either heatmap has a standardised residual beyond ±2, so no single segment and class combination stands out: any difference in SEC or AGE is spread thinly across the table."
} else {
  str_glue("The cells that drive the SEC and AGE results are: ",
           str_flatten_comma(str_glue_data(strong_cells,
             "{map_chr(cluster, seg_label)} has {if_else(resid > 0, 'more', 'fewer')} {variable} {level} households than expected ({sprintf('%+.1f', resid)})"),
             ", and "), ".")
}
pairs_text <- if (nrow(sig_pairs) == 0) {
  "For household size, no pair of segments differs once the p-values are adjusted for multiple comparisons."
} else {
  str_glue("For household size, the pairs that differ after adjustment are ",
           str_flatten_comma(str_glue_data(sig_pairs, "segments {group2} and {group1} ({fmt_p(p.value)})"), ", and "), ".")
}

cat("\n\n", cells_text, " ", pairs_text,
    " These are the comparisons a client should rely on when deciding which segment to approach with which offer.\n\n", sep = "")
```

## Did we miss a better demographic? {#sec-profile-check}

The three variables were chosen for business reasons. As a check, every demographic is measured on how strongly it separates the segments, using one common measure, Cramér's V. Numeric variables (HS, Affluence and EDU, which has nine sparse levels) are first cut into four equal-sized groups, and native-language codes held by fewer than 20 households are pooled, so that rare codes do not inflate the measure.

```{r}
#| label: profile-all-demographics
#| eval: true

all_demo_v <- map_dfr(demo_cols, \(v) {
  d <- soap_clusters |>
    select(MemberID, cluster) |>
    left_join(soap_clean |> select(MemberID, value = all_of(v)), by = "MemberID") |>
    filter(!is.na(value))
  grp <- if (v %in% c("HS", "Affluence", "EDU")) {
    factor(ntile(d$value, 4))                      # numeric: four equal-sized groups
  } else {
    fct_lump_min(factor(d$value), min = 20)         # categorical: pool rare codes
  }
  tab <- table(d$cluster, grp)
  res <- suppressWarnings(chisq.test(tab))         # only the statistic is used
  tibble(variable = v, n = nrow(d),
         cramers_v = cramers_v(tab, unname(res$statistic)),
         chosen = v %in% profile_vars)
})

all_demo_v |>
  ggplot(aes(cramers_v, fct_reorder(variable, cramers_v), fill = chosen)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = pal[1], `FALSE` = pal[6]),
                    labels = c(`TRUE` = "Chosen", `FALSE` = "Not chosen")) +
  labs(title = "How strongly each demographic separates the segments",
       x = "Cramér's V", y = NULL, fill = NULL)
```

```{r}
#| label: profile-check-text
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| results: asis

# One line reason for leaving each other demographic out (from the section above)
why_not <- c(Affluence = "it largely repeats SEC and has more missing values",
             MT = "its codes have no labels, so a difference cannot be turned into an action",
             CHILD = "its categories have no labels in the data guide",
             SEX = "almost every homemaker is female, so it cannot guide targeting",
             EDU = "it has many sparse levels and is less directly tied to a soap decision",
             FEH = "eating habits have no clear link to how bath soap is sold",
             CS = "it only records television availability")

weakest_chosen <- all_demo_v |> filter(chosen)  |> slice_min(cramers_v, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)
best_other     <- all_demo_v |> filter(!chosen) |> slice_max(cramers_v, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)

cat("\n\n", if (best_other$cramers_v <= weakest_chosen$cramers_v) {
  str_glue("All three chosen variables separate the segments at least as well as any of the others ",
           "(the strongest of the rest, {best_other$variable}, has V = {round(best_other$cramers_v, 3)}), ",
           "so the choice is supported by the data as well as by business sense.")
} else {
  str_glue("{best_other$variable} separates the segments more than {weakest_chosen$variable} ",
           "(V = {round(best_other$cramers_v, 3)} against {round(weakest_chosen$cramers_v, 3)}). ",
           "It was still left out because {why_not[[best_other$variable]]}. ",
           "It is reported here so a reader can see the trade-off rather than take the choice on trust.")
}, "\n\n", sep = "")
```

## Summary table

```{r}
#| label: profile-summary

profile_summary <- profile_df |>
  group_by(cluster) |>
  summarise(
    households = n(),
    sec_high   = mean(as.integer(SEC) <= 2),            # SEC 1 or 2
    sec_low    = mean(as.integer(SEC) == 4),            # SEC 4
    hs_median  = median(HS, na.rm = TRUE),
    hs_mean    = mean(HS, na.rm = TRUE),
    age_old    = mean(AGE == "4 Old")                   # oldest homemaker group
  )

profile_summary |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_percent(c(sec_high, sec_low, age_old), decimals = 0) |>
  fmt_number(hs_mean, decimals = 1) |>
  cols_label(cluster = "Segment", households = "Households",
             sec_high = "SEC 1 or 2", sec_low = "SEC 4",
             hs_median = "Median size", hs_mean = "Mean size",
             age_old = "Homemaker AGE 4") |>
  tab_spanner(label = "Socioeconomic class", columns = c(sec_high, sec_low)) |>
  tab_spanner(label = "Household size", columns = c(hs_median, hs_mean)) |>
  tab_header(title = "Demographic profile of each segment")
```

```{r}
#| results: asis

# Each segment is compared with the average household to suggest a price, pack and media focus
overall <- profile_df |>
  summarise(sec_high = mean(as.integer(SEC) <= 2), hs_mean = mean(HS, na.rm = TRUE),
            age_old = mean(AGE == "4 Old"))

lines <- profile_summary |>
  mutate(
    label = map_chr(cluster, seg_label),
    price = if_else(sec_high > overall$sec_high, "a premium range", "a value range and price promotions"),
    pack  = if_else(hs_mean  > overall$hs_mean,  "larger packs and multi-packs", "standard packs"),
    media = if_else(age_old  > overall$age_old,  "television and in-store", "digital channels")
  ) |>
  str_glue_data("- **{label}** ({households} households): {pct(sec_high)} in SEC 1 or 2, a median household ",
                "of {hs_median} members and {pct(age_old)} with the oldest homemakers. ",
                "Suggested focus: {price}, {pack}, and {media}.")

act_vars <- profile_tests |> filter(actionable) |> pull(variable)

cat("\n\nPutting the three demographics together gives a short profile of each segment:\n\n",
    paste(lines, collapse = "\n"), "\n\n",
    if (length(act_vars) == 0) {
      "These suggestions are only a starting point: none of the three demographics differed clearly between segments, so the purchase behaviour in section 2(d) should lead the targeting and the demographics only fine-tune it."
    } else {
      str_glue("The suggestions carry most weight for {str_flatten_comma(act_vars, ' and ')}, {if (length(act_vars) == 1) 'the only variable whose test' else 'the variables whose tests'} showed a real difference. {if (length(act_vars) < 3) 'The rest should be treated as a secondary guide.' else ''}")
    }, "\n\n", sep = "")
```
